source.title: Open Problems in Heavy Quarkonium Physics

accepted.question_text: What is the correct chromoelectric correlator governing the dominant non-perturbative correction to heavy-quarkonium masses, and does an accurate determination of that correlator support or invalidate a perturbative treatment of the bottomonium ground state? In the framework discussed in the paper, the non-perturbative mass shift depends on the correlator hE(t)E(0)i(μ); existing quenched lattice estimates give an inverse correlation length of about 1.25 GeV, a scale that is not only larger than the typical binding-energy scale E but also comparable to the momentum-transfer scale p. The open problem is therefore to determine this correlator accurately enough to decide whether the apparent success of perturbative calculations for the ground-state bottomonium system is genuinely justified.
accepted.context_brief: Chromoelectric correlator and bottomonium ground state

evidence.quote: A precise determination of this formula would need having an accurate determination of the chromoelectric correlator.
This may potentially question the whole perturbative approach to the ground state of bottomonium.
Only a better determination of the chromoelectric correlator can solve the conundrum.

accepted.question_text: How should the ground-state bottomonium hyperfine splitting be determined once next-to-next-to-leading-order effects are included, and what value should be expected experimentally? The paper notes that no experimental data were yet available for bottomonium hyperfine splittings and that NNLO effects are potentially important because both non-perturbative contributions, relevant when ΛQCD is of order E, and mass-correction effects first enter at that order. The open problem is to produce a quantitatively reliable prediction, including these corrections, and confront it with measurement.

evidence.quote: In the bottomonium case there are not yet experimental data.
We note, however, that NNLO corrections may be potentially important for this observable, also considering that at this order new type of corrections will appear for the first time:
• non-perturbative corrections, which are parametrically of NNLO in the situation ΛQCD ∼ E.

accepted.question_text: Are the approximately equal radial spacings seen in the low-lying bottomonium spectrum merely a numerical coincidence of perturbative calculations with leading-order renormalon cancellation, or do they genuinely reflect that these states are Coulombic or quasi-Coulombic bound states? Resolving this requires further theoretical and phenomenological study of higher bottomonium levels and their fine splittings.

evidence.quote: If this is coincidental or reflects the (quasi-)Coulombic nature of the states will be decided by further studies.

It seems to indicate either the existence of large NLL/NNLO corrections (as it happens in the hyperfine splittings of the 1S levels) or sizeable non-perturbative corrections, somehow hidden in the error bands of Fig. 2.

accepted.question_text: What are the next-to-leading-order contributions in the heavy-quark velocity expansion to the inclusive decay widths of the χcJ states, and once those contributions are computed, can the improved decay-width ratios be used to determine αs at the charm-mass scale? The paper explains that existing data are already sensitive to NLO corrections in the Wilson coefficients, but that a consistent extraction of αs requires the velocity-expansion corrections because they may be as large as those perturbative corrections.
accepted.context_brief: χc inclusive decays and αs extraction

evidence.quote: Clearly the data have become sensitive to NLO corrections and may be used, in principle, to determine αs at the charm-mass scale.

Before this, a necessary step is the calculation of the decay widths at next-to-leading order in the velocity expansion, since these contributions are potentially of the same magnitude as NLO corrections in the Wilson coefficients.

accepted.question_text: Why do Tevatron measurements of high-transverse-momentum charmonium production fail to show the transverse polarization expected from standard NRQCD gluon-fragmentation dynamics? In the scenario described in the paper, large-pT production is dominated by a transversely polarized gluon fragmenting into a color-octet 3S1 heavy-quark pair, and standard NRQCD power counting predicts that this transverse polarization should survive into the observed S-wave quarkonium state. The open problem is whether the discrepancy is due to experimental uncertainty, alternative power counting, or higher-order effects that dilute the polarization.

evidence.quote: In this section we briefly mention two of the main open problems in our understanding of charmonium production.
The present Tevatron data [53] do not seem to confirm this expectation.
The uncertainties are, however, too large to make any definite claim. The issue here is mainly experimental and more precise Tevatron data are eagerly awaited.

accepted.question_text: What theoretical mechanism can explain the unexpectedly large double-charmonium production rates observed by Belle in e+e− annihilation, particularly for inclusive J/ψ + c c̄ and exclusive J/ψ + ηc final states, whose measured cross sections are nearly an order of magnitude larger than available predictions? The paper notes that the Belle upper bound on J/ψ + J/ψ remains compatible with theory, so the open problem is to identify what ingredient is missing in the theoretical description of the channels that disagree with data and whether a genuinely new production mechanism is required.

evidence.quote: The most challenging open problem in charmonium production concerns double charmonium production in e+e− annihilations.
are far by almost an order of magnitude from the available theoretical predictions:
Even if independent data by BaBar would be most welcome, the issue here seems to be mainly theoretical and the data may be the signal of some new production mechanism.
